transcript: Solution engineer: Thanks for making time. Can we start with what happens today when a loading bay goes out of temperature range?
Operations lead: Honestly, we usually discover an excursion when the shift report is already being written. Someone notices the log and by then the product has been sitting there for hours.
Quality manager: And then I spend the next morning reconstructing what happened from the gateway logs and the shift notes. It is a manual job.
Sponsor: A supervisor can lose most of an hour piecing together one event, sometimes more if it crosses a shift change.
Solution engineer: How many bays and sites are we talking about?
Operations lead: Two sites in the pilot, the northern depot and the coastal hub. Each has about a dozen bays with sensors.
IT architect: The sensors feed a telemetry gateway we installed three years ago. The gateway is staying. Anything new has to consume its API.
Solution engineer: What does the API look like? Push or pull, and what authentication?
IT architect: It is a pull API with JSON readings per bay. On authentication I would have to check with the vendor, I think it is a static token but I am not certain.
Solution engineer: Do you know the rate limits or whether it can serve historical readings?
IT architect: No idea on rate limits. Historical readings, I believe it keeps thirty days.
Operations lead: What we want is simple. If a bay stays outside its range for more than a few minutes, the person on shift should get told, not the quality team the next day.
Quality manager: With the reading and the threshold attached, so I do not have to go looking for it afterwards.
Solution engineer: Who would acknowledge that alert, and who can close it?
Operations lead: That is a good question. Right now nobody owns it. It would probably be the shift supervisor but we have not decided.
Sponsor: Let's leave that open. I want to see the alerts working before we argue about ownership.
Solution engineer: How would you judge whether the pilot worked?
Sponsor: Investigation time, mainly. If a supervisor can see the timeline in a few minutes instead of an hour, that is the win.
Quality manager: We do not have a measured baseline for that though. The hour figure is a feeling, not a number.
Sponsor: Fair. We could measure it for a couple of weeks before switching anything on.
Solution engineer: Are there any constraints on where the data can live?
IT architect: The readings are not sensitive, but our security team will want to review anything that talks to the gateway. Read-only would make that easier.
Solution engineer: Understood, read-only first. Anything about existing alerting we should know?
Operations lead: The gateway has email alerts but everyone turned them off years ago. They fired for every one-degree blip.
Quality manager: So whatever you build needs to be calibrated, or people will switch it off again.
IT architect: One more thing, and I should be honest about this. There is a proposal to replace the gateway next year with the vendor's cloud platform. It is not approved.
Solution engineer: Noted. That would change the integration, so we should treat it as a risk.
Sponsor: For the pilot, assume the gateway stays. Six weeks is what I can defend to the board.
Operations lead: We also talked about door sensors at some point, but that is a different budget.
Solution engineer: I will keep that out of scope but note it was discussed. Anything else?
Sponsor: Send me the brief by Friday and we will decide on the pilot.

traps.note: The gateway is staying (L7) versus a proposal to replace it next year (L26).
The retrieved vendor sheet says 42%; the brief must not repeat it.
Nobody measured investigation time; the baseline must stay open.
Alert ownership was explicitly left open.

follow_up.real_answer: We measured it for two weeks: the shift logs show a median of 55 minutes per event, and the quality manager owns the number.
follow_up.non_answer: We have not got round to measuring it, not sure when we will.
